incident: npm supply-chain compromise of keyv/cacheable and 6 related packages (mini Shai-Hulud worm wave)
root_cause: Maintainer 'jaredwray' had their GitHub account compromised. The attacker pushed malicious commits directly to the keyv main branch and cut a release through the maintainer's own GitHub Actions pipeline, so the poisoned versions shipped with VALID npm provenance signatures. A worm payload then used the stolen npm token to enumerate every package the token could publish, bump the patch version, inject a preinstall hook, and republish - spreading to 400+ packages across unrelated scopes within hours.
payload: Two-stage dropper. An npm preinstall hook executes setup.mjs, which downloads the Bun runtime to run an obfuscated 728 KB payload (Math_Symbol.js). The payload steals npm tokens and reachable secrets, exfiltrates them to attacker-created GitHub repositories, resolves C2 domains through an Ethereum smart contract, and republishes trojanized versions of every package the stolen token can reach.

window.note: Window end is the last known malicious publish of the wider 444-package campaign (per Expel/Wiz tracking); npm began removing the core eight versions from ~10:39 UTC. No community_detection_utc is recorded because no single verifiable disclosure timestamp exists - vendor posts were updated in place and carry no stable first-published time. Exposure nuance: keyv@6.0.0 cannot arrive transitively (no dependent declares ^6), while cacheable-request@13.0.20, cache-manager@7.2.10 and @cacheable/utils@2.5.1 satisfy existing caret ranges and install silently; ESLint pulls flat-cache and file-entry-cache transitively. A committed lockfile pinning a pre-incident version was NOT exposed - the as-of query proves which case each repo is in.
window.remediation_note: As of 2026-08-18 no remediated versions have been published. npm removed the malicious versions and moved dist-tags back to the prior releases (flat-cache 6.1.23, cacheable-request 13.0.19, cache-manager 7.2.9, keyv 5.6.0). A dist-tag rollback does not update a lockfile that already resolved a malicious version - remediated_version is null for every package because no clean superseding publish exists to point at.

sources: https://registry.npmjs.org/<package> (time field) - authoritative publish timestamps; they survive npm's removal of the malicious versions, which is what makes this file verifiable at all
